But the answer is to address housing supply, infrastructure, services and the composition of the migration intake, he will say.

According to OECD research across Australia’s regions, in places where more migrants arrived, employment among Australian-born workers grew faster, not slower, with no measurable effect on their wages.
Related: Sydney travelled, learned a trade and found love in Australia. It might have been a different story under Labor’s migration plan
Without migration, Australia’s working-age population would decrease as the number of older people grows.

“An ageing country that chooses to shrink its working-age population while promising to spend more on health, care and defence has not developed a plan – it has put forward a contradiction,” Cormann will say.

Tariffs, which have been imposed by US president Donald Trump and proposed by One Nation, would also fail to address the cost of living and could instead raise costs for farmers, miners and builders, Cormann will say.
He believes Australia can only grow its way out of the issue through productivity.
“There is no shortcut to a lower cost of living. There is no populist shortcut, through tariffs and caps and state banks,” he will say.
“There is only the long way round: an economy that produces more, competes harder and grows faster than its costs … anyone offering you a quicker route is offering you a poorer country.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia building non-negotiable ‘security zone’ inside Ukrainian border, Putin declares
articles.summary: Russian president says area will not be part of any potential peace talks while Kremlin puts its size at spanning 660km. What we know on day 1,697
body: Russia is establishing a “security zone” inside Ukraine along the border and it will be non-negotiable in any ⁠future talks with Kyiv, Vladimir Putin has said. The Russian president, wearing military uniform and speaking during a visit to a command post, said the operation ⁠was in response to Ukraine’s ⁠2024-25 incursion into ​Russia’s western Kursk region. “The Russian armed forces were tasked not only with expelling the enemy from our land but also with establishing a security zone ⁠in the adjacent territory. This task is being carried out successfully,” he said in televised comments on Friday. “Our goal is to ensure the absolute security of Russia’s border regions ⁠for the future, and we do not plan to make this a subject for potential peace negotiations with ​Ukraine.”

The planned ‌security zone spanned 660km (410 ‌miles), of which 70% was currently under Russia’s control, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said. Peskov did not say how deep it would ‌reach inside Ukraine. The zone requires Russia to carve out land in the Sumy and Kharkiv regions, which are not among those it is illegally claiming as its own territory.

Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling the US Congress the pause on the legislation which passed both chambers was in the national interest. The US president said in an executive order on Friday he was waiving many ⁠sanctions, restrictions and duties ⁠on Russia, in a move that comes as he has been publicly criticising ⁠Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Zelenskyy said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service had not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House. Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels and asked the EU for another €70bn ($79bn/£59bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia, report Jennifer Rankin and Andrew Roth. Hours earlier Trump called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” after his purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.

Russian attacks killed at least eight people and injured 60 ⁠across Ukraine on Friday, hit two shopping centres and cut power to more than 1 million people after strikes on the energy grid, ⁠officials said. Two were kiled and 12 more wounded in attacks on three districts of the eastern city of Kharkiv, governor Oleh Syniehubov ⁠said. Further Russian strikes through the evening injured nine, officials said. Attacks in Kramatorsk in the eastern Donetsk region killed two and another two were killed in south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.

A drone strike on a food-processing facility killed one person and wounded eight in the north-western region of Volyn, according to governor Roman Romaniuk, leaving 370,000 people temporarily without power. Drone attacks also struck a customs terminal ​and torched about 10 trucks in the town of Kovel, he said. Other attacks hit at least two shopping centres – one in the northern city of Sumy and another in the neighbouring region of ⁠Rivne, officials said.

The attacks came as a new report showed that civilian casualties from Russia’s invasion have climbed steeply. At least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 wounded last month – a total that is 85% higher than in September last year, the report from the UN human rights office in Kyiv said on Friday. It said intensifying Russian attacks in October already had killed dozens of civilians, including children. “The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years,” said Danielle Bell, the UN office head.

As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian, writes Andrew Roth in this analysis.

articles.title: Uncovering the secrets of New Zealand’s elusive ‘jungle penguins’
articles.summary: The tawaki, or Fiordland crested penguin, known for its prominent yellow eyebrows, has for years baffled scientists with its unusual habits
body: Deep in the misty fjords of New Zealand’s South Island, a team of researchers is trying to catch one of the world’s most elusive penguins: the forest-dwelling tawaki, or Fiordland crested penguin.For weeks, researchers stand sentry each day over a burrow on Eleanor Island, hoping to corner the female bird so they can retrieve data from its tagging device.
But this penguin has developed a clever exit strategy – digging multiple tunnels to elude its captors.
The Tutoko I prepares for a research trip during its annual Fiordland crested penguin nest survey around Doubtful Sound

“It took us about four days to recapture that bird,” says Dr Thomas Mattern, a research fellow at the University of Otago and chair of the Tawaki Project, a scientific initiative established to study the population.
“We plugged all the holes around the nest so that it could not escape, until we finally could recover that device,” he adds.
In a first for the species, Tawaki Project researchers are conducting long-term population counts, unlocking secrets about the bird’s breeding and foraging habits, and what threats they might face.

The project is New Zealand’s most comprehensive mapping of tawaki nests. Over September, it mapped 93 nests across two islands in Fiordland, and has now mapped 1,200 nests across nine fjords in the past 12 years. Its mapping shows the tawaki population is roughly three times bigger than earlier surveys suggest, says Mattern, pictured below at Precipice Cove.
Dr Thomas Mattern searches for tawaki near Precipice Cove during a research trip with the Tawaki Project

The Māori name for crested penguins, tawaki, is a catch-all for several species around New Zealand and the sub-Antarctic region, but the focus of this annual voyage is on the declining species that inhabits remote Fiordland, New Zealand’s largest national park, which is Unesco heritage listed.

Until German-born Mattern and his wife, Ursula Ellenberg, founded the volunteer research project in 2014, almost nothing was known about Fiordland’s tawaki, which stands half a metre tall, and features prominent yellow eyebrows.
“Tawaki are a ghost,” Mattern says of the penguin’s enigmatic behaviour.
But “they are the most amazing penguin species … They do not fit any penguin mould. What we know about penguins, you throw it all out of the window.”
Clockwise from top left: A tawaki taking shelter. A research vessel at anchor near the Shelter Islands. Dr Thomas Mattern looks for penguins. A nest tag on Eleanor Island

Unlike most penguins, the Fiordland tawaki do not breed in colonies, preferring instead to build single burrows deep in dense rainforest, sometimes at high elevations. While some other species can nest in forests, tawaki are unique because they nest exclusively in forests, Mattern says, describing them as “proper jungle penguins”.
Its hunting habits are also unusual. Some groups fish entirely within the fjords, while others hunt in the ocean.
The tawaki’s habits have baffled scientists
“When you think you have them nailed down, you go to a different fjord, and they show behaviour that just does not conform to any of the ideas you have developed so far,” Mattern says.
Related: Myth or mystery: are moose roaming the isolated wilds of New Zealand?

Tawaki have also become infamous among scientists for their baffling journey to feed before they go through their annual “catastrophic moult” – the scientific term for when animals shed and replace all their feathers in one go.

All penguins moult after breeding season and before they do, they eat vast quantities of food to put on weight. Despite an abundance of food around the fjords in December (when breeding season ends), tawaki undertake a 5,000 to 7,000km return trip to the sub-Antarctic region to feed.

“These emaciated tawaki, that have just said goodbye to their chicks, hop in the water and travel halfway to Antarctica, which makes absolutely zero sense because there should be more than enough food in the water just outside their breeding area,” Mattern says.
“They are running a marathon, while trying to gain weight.”
Researchers Owen Dabkowski and Mandy Abernethy explore a nest on Eleanor Island
Mattern believes tawaki are likely acting on ancient instinct, heading to grounds where all other crested penguin species feed.
The Tawaki Project is funded by public donations and international grants, and supported by local volunteers, such as
Related: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
Richard Abernathy, the owner of tourism company Fiordland Expeditions, who donates his boat and time to the expedition for several weeks a year.
“Since 2018, we’ve been chasing penguins all over Fiordland,” says Abernathy whose ability to find nests in surprising places has earned him the nickname “sniffer dog”.
Together, their efforts have “shed light on the most understudied species” in New Zealand, Mattern says.

In 2020, the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List moved tawaki up in status from “vulnerable” to “near-threatened” because the researchers were able to develop a better picture of their populations, estimated to be in the region of 12,00 to 15,000 mature birds.
A tawaki swims in Charles Sound in Fiordland
But risks remain, including from commercial fishing practices.
“[We’re] looking at survival rates … to determine whether the population is stable,” says Mattern.
“If they’re going down, then we need to kick into gear to improve the situation for them.”

articles.title: China’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishes
articles.summary: The concept of ‘paying to suffer’ soars in popularity, with simulated disasters proving a modern twist on visiting sites of historic tragedies
body: When Leon Lv was looking for somewhere to travel last year, she turned to the Chinese social media app RedNote for ideas. The algorithm took her to videos of people struggling to survive typhoon-strength winds and flash floods.

“I never experienced a typhoon. I don’t know how it will feel and what will happen. I just have seen it on the news,” says the 28-year-old from Chongqing in south-west China. “So that’s why I want to go there to have a safe place to experience it and learn something.”
She travelled more than 1,300km to Hangzhou in the east, and joined a group of 20 to take part in a disaster simulation that featured a typhoon-fuelled flooding scenario.

Standing in a simulated flood, her mind momentarily went blank as hundreds of tonnes of water swept people off their feet, and carried them towards a safety barrier. As the surge hit, she forgot she was in a simulation. “One thing I learned is how to stay calm and protect myself during a flood. I learned how to use the right body position to stay safe,” she says. “No book and no school [can] teach me like that.”
Across Chinese social platforms phrases like “paying to suffer”, or “paying to buy fear” are trending online as part of a wave of interest in experiences known as “dark tourism”.
Lvxing Base, a company in Hangzhou offering simulated disaster experiences has gone viral. The founders spent 10 years making documentaries in some of the world’s most extreme environments.

At a 200,000 square metre facility, which opened in 2024, they simulate extreme weather conditions like typhoons and mudslides, giving participants the experience of what it would be like in a disaster.

“I don’t deny that many people come because they want excitement,” says general manager Wang Kuanghan. They want to see what this place is like, what a real typhoon and torrential rain feel like, and whether they themselves can withstand it. Most of our individual customers are between 20 and 30 years old.”
It plans to open five more centres across China within the next three years. It also plans to create earthquake and fire simulations.

The offering are not limited to private companies. At Beijing’s Haidian public safety museum, tourists experience simulated earthquakes, tsunamis and fires using a 4D theatre, equipped with moving platforms and sound effects. Last year the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou opened a five-storey centre to teach visitors how to respond to emergencies and disasters. Its earthquake simulator can recreate ground shaking equivalent to a 7.2 magnitude quake.

Extreme weather has become increasingly common in China. In 2025, China recorded its highest number of hot days since records began, and was hit by 10 typhoons, well above the long-term annual average. China’s ministry of emergencies reported that 67 million people were affected by such disasters across the country.

In 2024, local governments were instructed to promote immersive disaster education, instructing safety centres, museums and training bases to use simulations to teach people how to respond in a real crisis.

“The new generation of Chinese travellers want to experience a place rather than simply see famous attractions,” says Robert Li, director of the School of Hotel and Tourism Management at the Chinese University of Hong Kong.
But some travellers have found a way to blend the two approaches; rather than indulging in the white-knuckle ride of a simulated typhoon, they are travelling to real sites of death and destruction.

In May 2008 a magnitude 8.0 earthquake devastated towns in China’s Sichuan province, killing more than 70,000 people. Alice*, a 30-year-old writer from Sichuan walked around Beichuan, one of the affected towns, the ruins of which the government had preserved. Metal beams hold collapsed buildings in place for the public to visit. She saw the site where schools collapsed, crushing students inside.
In Yingxue close to the epicentre, a broken clock surrounded by the remains of a middle school is frozen at 2.28, the moment the earthquake struck.

“I felt scared because of the power of nature and how many children and students could not escape from it,” says Alice, who plans to start a Chinese language Substack account detailing her journeys into tragedy. “Everything was so broken. It became like a ghost town, because nobody lives in the old town any more.”
Alice believes dark tourism helps a country reconcile with its past, even if the government decides what can be remembered.

In recent years, tour guide Samantha Wang has seen an increase in Chinese tourists attending the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall. In 1937 the Japanese Imperial army captured Nanjing, and Chinese official accounts say 300,000 civilians and soldiers were killed over weeks of massacres. Japan’s official position is that it acknowledges that large numbers of civilians were killed but says the number of victims is “difficult to determine”.
Entry to the hall is free but tourists must book online The local government reserves 25,000 places a day. In August, tickets to attend the museum are frequently sold out in advance, she says.
“There are more tragic sites in China, and I see more people interested to know about that. That’s a new trend” says Wang.

Inside the memorial hall hang photos of victims. “They [visitors] feel sad when they see those pictures, when they see those kids who were killed … After the visit, they feel relieved, and they feel encouraged that they should work harder to make China stronger,” she says.
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li in Taipei

articles.title: Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy
articles.summary: Ukrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White House
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House.
Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels, where he asked the EU for another €70bn (£60bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia.

The meeting offered an important opportunity for Zelenskyy and Europe to align their strategies, as Zelenskyy once again found himself embroiled in a major quarrel with the US president, Donald Trump.
Related: Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’

Hours earlier, Trump had called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised ⁠Zelenskyy, after a purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.
“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told the Newsmax television channel. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace.”
Energy analysts told the BBC that the US-Israeli war on Iran was having the biggest impact on diesel export volumes, although the Ukraine war was also significant.

Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph. Neither has officially been confirmed.
Speaking after meeting EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy said that Starshield had not yet returned to normal.

“Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities,” Zelenskyy said. “Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.”

Reuters on Friday reported that the order to throttle Starshield had come from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a western official briefed on the matter. They did not identify the White House official who had made the decision, but said the Pentagon had been informed that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military had to be slowed.
Trump said on Friday he did not think either ⁠he or ⁠Elon ​Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starshield access and that any limits were not imposed by the US.
Starshield is produced by Musk’s SpaceX but controlled by the US government.

Zelenskyy called it a “very dangerous and unpleasant surprise” that speeds had been reduced on Starlink, which Ukraine uses to support its most effective air defence systems against Russian jet-powered drones.
Russian attacks killed at least eight people and injured 60 ⁠across Ukraine on Friday, hitting two shopping centres and temporarily power to more than 1 million people, ⁠officials said.

When Zelenskyy arrived for talks with EU leaders, he was applauded by the heads of state and government of the bloc’s 27 countries. Zelenskyy later said he had heard “only support”, when asked about reports that European leaders had asked him to dial down his criticism of Trump.

According to a transcript of his remarks, he told EU leaders that the war would cost €155bn in 2027. “And we need at least €70bn more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience,” he said. “This is a realistic amount.”

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, agreed with Zelenskyy that “it is clear that we have a gap of €70bn that has to be covered” for 2027, although she expected Ukraine’s other partners – which she did not name – to cover part of the sum.

The EU is currently giving Ukraine regular payments from a €90bn funding plan agreed last December that was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s civilian and military needs for 2026-27. The remaining third was to be filled by other “international partners”, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan.

The realisation that Kyiv again risks a financial crunch has put Russia’s €210bn assets frozen inside the EU back on the table. The EU takes the profits from those assets to support Ukraine, but last year decided against using the funds themselves, instead opting for an EU-backed €90bn loan.

Belgium, which hosts the vast majority of the Russian funds, remains strongly opposed to using the frozen assets, fearing it will be left to carry the financial burden if the plan goes wrong. But Zelenskyy said there could be an alternative.

“We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war,” he said.

The European Commission, a strong backer of last year’s rejected frozen assets plan, has been reluctant to propose new variants – such as an EU-controlled custodian – because it fears running into same opposition from Belgium and other sceptical member states.

Before the summit, Belgium’s prime minister, Bart De Wever, said Zelenskyy would “probably look everybody straight in the eye and say: thank you for the €90bn, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing”.

articles.title: Brazil’s Lula says he now backs lowering age of criminal responsibility to 16
articles.summary: Lula reverses position on age of responsibility for ‘heinous’ crimes in what many see as a desperate electoral gambit
body: Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced that he now supports lowering the age of criminal responsibility for “heinous” crimes from 18 to 16, reversing a longstanding policy in what is widely seen as a desperate electoral gambit.

The U-turn, which Lula announced during a Thursday night interview with TV Globo, comes with the presidential runoff in just over a week. The incumbent faces an uphill battle to overturn the first-round victory of his opponent, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who remains slightly ahead at the polls.

Both the senator and his father, the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, have long supported lowering the age of criminal responsibility – they want it reduced to 14 rather than 16 – but Lula and his party have always opposed the change.

After repeated opinion polls, the latest of them this week, showed that 80% of the population supports lowering the age, Lula said: “My view, as a Brazilian citizen, is that for any and every heinous crime, I am in favour of lowering the age.”
He answered “yes” when the reporter asked whether he meant lowering it to 16.

The list of crimes classified as “heinous” under Brazilian law is extensive, ranging from murder and rape to the falsification of medicines and drug trafficking – the offence for which about a quarter of the 816,000 people serving prison sentences in Brazil were incarcerated.

Human rights organisations and security experts have long criticised proposals to lower the age of criminal responsibility, arguing that they do little to tackle violence while increasing recruitment into organised crime in Brazil’s overcrowded prisons.

On Thursday, before Lula’s interview, the proposal had been discussed in the senate. The Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation, had criticised it for “not addressing the causes of violence”, adding that placing young people “prematurely in the prison system tends to deepen cycles of violence and exclusion, undermining their rehabilitation”.

The columnist Josias de Souza wrote in his UOL column that, by reversing his longstanding position, Lula “decided to change himself. It was no ordinary transformation. On public security, Lula turned himself inside out. He began defending what he had always rejected.”

The incumbent has doubled down in recent days in an effort to overturn Bolsonaro’s 2.2 million-vote first-round lead by appealing to independents and undecided voters. He has secured congressional approval for a shorter working week – a proposal on which Bolsonaro himself U-turned and decided to support at the last minute, when it appeared ready to pass – and debt relief for microentrepreneurs, as well as promising free public transport on weekends.

articles.title: Israeli settlers attack olive farmers and Washington Post journalist in West Bank
articles.summary: Settlers hurl rocks at Palestinians and beat photographer Heidi Levine as part of yearly attacks to disrupt harvest
body: Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians across the occupied West Bank in a coordinated movement to disrupt the annual olive harvest, burning cars and trees and injuring Palestinians and a Washington Post photographer.

Masked settlers wielding clubs and other weapons attacked people attempting to harvest their olives in West Bank towns on Friday. Palestinian authorities said they recorded attacks in eight villages, and injuries among at least 20 people.

It was the latest series of attacks in a deadly campaign of Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in recent months, violence which has drawn accusations of “ethnic cleansing”, including from the British government.

In the town of Abu Falah, near Ramallah, at least 80 settlers, some of whom were carrying firearms or clubs, gathered to stop Palestinians from harvesting their olives, using slingshots to hurl rocks at the farmers in view of Israeli military vehicles. When some of the Palestinians then picked up rocks to defend themselves, the Israeli military fired teargas in their direction.

The Israeli Foreign Press Association said in a statement: “This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities.”

Among those injured was the Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was beaten by settlers in an attack that lasted more than 10 minutes, according to witnesses. Settlers stole her passport, phone, wallet and equipment.

“I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me,” Levine said from a hospital bed in Ramallah. She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.
In a statement, the Washington Post said Levine had been wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist.

The office of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that the facts surrounding the attack on Levine were “unclear”, suggesting the attack was the fault of “200 Arabs and far-left activists” who confronted Israeli youths. The office added that it condemned “violence against anyone”.

There has been a surge of settler violence against Palestinians over the past month. Settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks since 27 September, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group.
Every year, settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest their olives, but there has been a rise in violence this year as Israel’s elections approach at the end of October.
At least four Palestinians had been killed and more than 100 others injured over the past month, Palestinian authorities said. Thousands of trees have been damaged.

Israel imposed new rules on the olive harvest this year, barring Palestinians from harvesting their trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.

The new orders prohibit Palestinians from entering about 8,800 hectares (21,800 acres) of agricultural land – a 30% increase from the year prior – without the approval of the Israeli military. By contrast, the military gave Israeli citizens access to more land this year.
Related: ‘They have total impunity’: West Bank settler violence surges after Gaza ceasefire

The rights group Peace Now says the military decreased the amount of land Israeli citizens were prohibited, for the purpose of preventing settler violence, from entering from about 1,070 hectares in 2025 to 680 hectares in 2026.

The olive harvest is an economic lifeline for Palestinians and has grown in importance since Israel revoked work permits for many Palestinians in the West Bank after the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023.
Photos and videos showed large swathes of agricultural land with uprooted olive trees in Kufur Malek, outside Ramallah, where Israeli bulldozers razed trees.

Settlers rarely face accountability for their violence, even when well-documented. Rights groups say settlers enjoy the protection of the Israeli military, which intervenes only if Palestinians try to defend themselves.
Netanyahu, has on occasion condemned the violence, which he says is due to just about 100 settlers, but he has taken few steps to stop it.

Settlements have rapidly expanded across the West Bank under his rightwing government, leading to international condemnation. The UN and most countries judge settlements to be in violation of international law.
Friday’s attack in Abu Falah followed a similar attack hours earlier near the West Bank village of Turmus Ayya, where settlers burned three cars after attacking Palestinians harvesting olives.
Videos shared by the Israeli rights group B’tselem showed hundreds of bags of olives “violently” stolen by Israeli settlers from Palestinians and taken to Israeli olive presses.
Sarit Michaeli, an independent activist, said settlers were stealing Palestinians’ olive crop on a scale “never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue”.
A spokesperson for the US embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack and declined to comment further due to privacy laws.

articles.title: India’s Cockroach Janta party leader arrested amid crackdown on protests
articles.summary: Abhijeet Dipke was detained before planned anti-government demonstrations in Delhi
body: The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday and then later formally arrested as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital.
Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in central Delhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.

On Saturday local media reported he was arrested “to prevent a breach of the peace”, with broadcasters NDTV and India Today saying he would be called before a special executive ⁠magistrate later in the day.
The Cockroach movement initially emerged back in May as online satire, but has since grown into one of the most substantial challenges to the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule.

Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims.

The authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend.

Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They were sentenced to five days in jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi.

At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and show Narendra Modi “that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.”

Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place.

When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying: “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was led away by dozens of police officers.
In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”
Neha Bora, a student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital.
Related: ‘How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?’: why Indian voters are on the streets

Despite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna, who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India was “on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”.

“We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.”
Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday.

The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said the BJP’s national spokesperson, Sambit Patra.
The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation.

In Mumbai, the Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.

articles.title: Power plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivable
articles.summary: Kremlin turning to punishment of Ukraine’s population in major cities as frontlines remain frozen
body: As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian.

Even as Donald Trump unilaterally declared an “energy ceasefire” last week between Moscow and Kyiv, Russia continued with its methodical and devastating strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, in particular in Kyiv, in a strategy meant to punish Ukraine’s population and drive the country to capitulation.
Related: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses

The potential goals of the Russian campaign, according to an assessment seen by the Guardian that Ukrainian intelligence said it intercepted from Russia last month, range from “degrading the quality of life” of Ukrainians through power outages to fully shutting off the water supply, which the document cooly predicts would cause the “deterioration of sanitary conditions and the forced outflow of residents from cities.”

The document does not specify which Russian agency developed the assessment, which is titled Analysis of Ukraine’s Energy, Housing and Utilities Sectors, includes vulnerable Ukrainian energy grid targets and even contemplates strikes against high-risk sites, including the switchyards at several nuclear power plants. But several European officials familiar with the document have said it is likely to have been produced by analytical departments linked to the Russian military or intelligence agencies, and that copies have circulated in Ukraine in previous years.

This year, however, Russia appears to be putting those plans into practice. On Tuesday night, Russian strikes hit three major power plants in the Kyiv region – Combined Heat and Power Plants 4 and 5, and the Trypillya Thermal Power Plant in the Kyiv region – as well as a major electrical substation that transfers electricity from two of the country’s main nuclear power plants to the capital. Those, along with other substations that make up the “Kyiv energy ring” that helps bring electricity from across the country to the capital, have all been targets of a Russian barrage that, if it succeeds, could threaten a humanitarian catastrophe in a city of 3 million people.

Ukraine’s energy minister first briefed European allies last month about the plan, a copy of which was first reported on by the New York Times. Russia has stepped up its attacks on the Ukrainian power grid precisely as Washington and Kyiv are embroiled in a major political quarrel. The Guardian is withholding some specifics of the military assessment at the request of Ukraine’s energy ministry, which said it could aid in further strikes against the country.

“There are two large documents, written very coldly and very clearly, with tables showing the number of weapons needed for each facility to destroy it,” Ukrainian energy minister Denys Shmyhal said last month. “The types of weapons range from ballistic missiles to jet-powered and conventional drones. We understand how they are going to act.”

The leaked documents identify bottlenecks and prescribe the number of ballistic and hypersonic cruise missiles and jet-powered drones needed to knock out power plants and substations with brutal efficiency. If that was done, it could destroy more than 90% of the power that Kyiv is budgeted for each winter, the document predicts, plunging the city into the dark and cold. A worst-case scenario could lead to blackouts lasting up to 20 hours a day until damaged equipment is repaired, according to expert projections.

The strikes on Ukraine’s energy system have become the country’s new frontlines – and the country is badly outgunned, as its stocks of US-provided PAC-3 missiles have dwindled. Zelenskyy this week castigated city authorities for poor planning for the winter and for failing to protect the city’s energy infrastructure. Protests over heat and electricity blackouts are also planned for Saturday, highlighting how the difficult conditions in winter could provoke a political crisis for the wartime government.

Economic Pravda, a leading Ukrainian news site that covers business, reported on Thursday that the three major power plants in Kyiv no longer have the ability to generate electricity, leaving the city more reliant on electricity brought from elsewhere in the country (the government generally does not confirm specific damage to critical infrastructure). The outlets’ experts predicted that, given a moderate winter and quick repairs of damaged substations, Kyiv residents could face up to eight hours of blackouts a day. Its worst case scenario of frigid temperatures and frequent attacks would leave Kyiv in the dark for up to 20 hours a day.

This is no accident for the Kremlin, which has increasingly turned to punishing Ukraine’s population in major cities as the frontlines of the conflict have frozen. “Last year, we were really on the brink,” said Volodymyr Fesenko, a Ukrainian political analyst. “But the risk this year will be even worse, so the plan [to attack Ukrainian infrastructure] does seem realistic. There’s a very high chance that Russia tries to break us this winter.” If the Kremlin believed in the chance of a clean military victory before now, he added, it may now believe that not to be possible, and focus on destroying Ukraine’s remaining infrastructure rather than trying to capture it.

The secret plan, which officials here say was intercepted by Ukrainian intelligence and then briefed to senior European diplomats by Shmyhal last month, sets itself several goals: to destroy electricity generation, heating, water and sewage systems in such a way as to to make life in Ukrainian cities unliveable. Destroying electrical generation alone, it says, would lead to a “significant decrease in the quality of life of the population.”

To do so, it specifies the number of weapons that should be allocated – Geran 4/5 jet-powered drones and hypersonic or cruise missiles – in order to destroy key infrastructure such as thermal power plants, substations, water pumping stations and more.
Considering strikes against the basis of Ukraine’s water, sewage and heating systems, the document says it would create a “large-scale municipal infrastructure crisis.”

When contacted by the Guardian, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry said that the document contained information that could aid in attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. It did not reply to questions on how the current Russian bombing strategy matched with the proposals made in the document, or which Russian agency had developed the plans.

articles.title: British man fined €3,000 for causing two-year-old son’s death in Cyprus
articles.summary: Joshua Foster pleaded guilty over death of toddler who fell from fourth-floor window of hotel during family holiday
body: A British man has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) after his two-year-old son fell 10 metres (33ft) to his death from the fourth-floor window of a hotel in Cyprus.
Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he approached it with the boy to show him the view of a waterpark and “lost control” of him, the court previously heard.
The 37-year-old appeared at Paphos district court on Friday for sentencing having pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.

In emotional scenes at the court, Judge Froso Christodoulidou ruled that Foster would not be jailed, before describing the incident on 12 July, the first day of the family’s holiday in Cyprus, as a “tragic event”.

“Jail is not appropriate,” the judge said, telling the courtroom that as there was “clearly no intent to kill” she had decided against a custodial sentence and would instead order Foster to pay the fine.

The Essex-born auditor, who had previously appeared in court visibly distraught, struggled to hold back tears as the sentence was handed down. As it dawned that the case was finally over, he hugged his lawyer before telling reporters: “Thank you for your support. I’m looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter.”

The light sentence – the minimum for the charge – meant Foster could retrieve his passport and other documents he had been forced to surrender. More usually levelled in cases involving fatal traffic accidents, the charge carries a maximum penalty of four years in prison.
Speaking outside the district court in Paphos, the defendant’s lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said Foster, who works for one of the UK’s big four accounting firms, would finally be able to grieve.

“He’s been through a lot and it’s been very emotional but he’s relieved it’s over,” he said of his client, who posted €30,000 in bail to return to the UK to attend the toddler’s funeral in August before being forced under threat of extradition to return to Cyprus for the proceedings.
“This case should not have gone to court. We asked for the charges to be suspended. Unfortunately this was not accepted.”

Alexandrou had appealed to the island’s attorney general, Cyprus’s top legal official, to discontinue the criminal procedure on humanitarian grounds, arguing that prosecution “does not serve the public interest”. The request was denied.
The boy fell to his death from the window of the King Evelthon hotel within hours of the family arriving in Paphos.

In mitigation on 5 October, Alexandrou recounted how Foster was making his way to a lift along the corridor when he stopped at the window and the “inconceivable” occurred. The Briton, he said, had not realised the window was ajar when, lifting the child, who was excitedly pointing to the hotel’s waterpark outside, he “lost control” and he slipped through his hands. The boy was pronounced dead at Paphos general hospital shortly after suffering severe cranial injuries when he hit a veranda below.
Summing up, Christodoulidou said while the presence of alcohol had been detected in Foster’s blood it was not enough to suggest he was impaired to the point where he had “acted recklessly”.

“It is no exaggeration to say that for the rest of his life he will have guilt for losing his child in such a tragic way,” she added. Mitigating factors presented by the defence, including the Briton’s lack of criminal record, as well as his guilty plea, had also played a role in her decision, she explained. In a country so dependent on tourism, criticism had mounted as Cypriot human rights defenders, media pundits and foreign diplomats all questioned the perceived lack of compassion with which officials approached the case.
A former British colony, the eastern Mediterranean island attracts roughly 4 million visitors and is particularly popular with tourists from the UK.

Alexandrou, the lawyer, said he had advised his client to admit the negligence charge to avoid a potentially drawn-out and disturbing trial when he and his family were still processing the grief of their “unimaginable loss”.

Conceding the case had been “emotional” for the entire defence team, the lawyer added: “He can finally grieve. Now that the court proceedings are over, the explosion of his emotions at the loss of his child will be immediate.”

In a statement issued after the sentencing, the Foster family said: “Today marks the end of the legal proceedings in Cyprus, and we are grateful to the court and Judge Christodoulidou for her decision to apply the maximum mitigation afforded to her.

“We are relieved that this process is now over, but for our family, the consequences of this tragedy will never end. Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day.
“Our focus now is on supporting one another and finding a way forward as a family. We ask that our privacy is respected as we do so.”

articles.title: Just 14% of Albertans want independence from Canada. Can a conference in a Calgary ballroom change that?
articles.summary: WeUnify’s Reclaiming Alberta brought together ardent supporters of separating from Canada while highlighting key disagreements – not least how close an independent Albert should be to the US
body: The debate began with a simple question in a dark Calgary hotel ballroom: does Alberta need Canada?

By the time the audience was asked to vote at the end, more than three-quarters had answered no – a decisive measure of the convictions of a room packed with some of Alberta’s most ardent independence supporters, some of whom had paid C$900 (£480) for a “visionary” weekend pass.

But outside the comfort of the ballroom, the debate is far from settled. Across the province, the forthcoming 19 October referendum on separatism has divided communities, prompting accusations of treason and grift and, at times, bitter feuds between former allies. One recent poll shows support for independence at only 14%.
You wouldn’t know it from the WeUnify’s Reclaiming Alberta conference though.

“This is a matter of survival,” conservative activist and broadcaster Faytene Grasseschi told the crowd, which erupted into applause after she said Alberta’s oil resources had been “usurped” by the federal government and the Canada she had been born into “doesn’t exist any more”.

In the main halls outside the ballroom, attendees milled around the vendor stalls. A handful donned a $6,500 (£4,925) helmet that resembles white colanders hastily attached to a bike helmet, bathing the user’s head in red LED light supposedly for treatment of “Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s, dementia, traumatic brain injury, [and] brain fog”. Others took in sales pitches about the need for gold and silver as paper money “fails”.

But the busiest stall belonged to the group Let’s Talk Alberta. It says it is neither a political party nor a campaign organisation but its five bound pamphlets include a 52-page volume titled Every Argument to Stay is a Reason to Leave. The pamphlets were written by its founder, Chris Scott, a cafe owner who attracted widespread attention during the Covid-19 pandemic after he was arrested for violating public health orders. After a lengthy legal battle, he was acquitted.

On stage, Scott told the crowd the push for independence would be a “wake-up call” for the rest of the country and reflected a fight against what many in the movement see as an entrenched political elite – a fight that needed to happen “come hell or high water”.

After initial efforts to bring a referendum question on independence were derailed by First Nations groups, Albertans will now be voting on the question of whether Alberta should remain part of Canada or whether the provincial government should begin the legal process to hold a second, binding referendum on separation. With just days to go, the foot soldiers and the faithful of the independence movement have begun their final pitches for what they envision will one day be a wealthy, “anti-woke” nation – one unshackled from the control of the federal government, or even a vassal of the United States.
Related: ‘Truly terrifying’: Alberta voter data breach raises fears for Canada’s electoral integrity

The conference, which was organised by the WeUnify movement, brought together Alberta separatists, veterans of the pandemic-era “freedom movement” and conservatives united by a distrust of established institutions.

Speakers reserved their harshest words for Justin Trudeau, who, despite resigning as prime minister more than a year ago, remains a bugbear for the separatist movement. Sheane Meikle, a volunteer with Let’s Talk Alberta, said the independence movement was gaining support.
“We’re getting far fewer Trudeau salutes when we wave flags on the side of the road,” he said – a reference to the raised middle finger.

Meikle, 58, has spent months travelling the province with Scott, adding more than 32,000 miles to his van as part of a quest to convince sceptical Albertans of the benefits of separation. The referendum had been “longtime coming” for the movement, he said. “Even if the results don’t go our way, it doesn’t mean we’re done. This is a movement now that’s sustained.”

Not everyone agreed the conference was the best idea, though. Keith Wilson, one of the principal intellectual and legal architects of Alberta’s modern separatist movement, admitted in an interview that he regretted participating. “It’s just an echo chamber in there – I’m not changing any minds that are already made up for separatism. I shouldn’t be here. I should be out campaigning.”
In September Wilson brought together 45 unnamed contributors to publish the Alberta Transition Plan, a 214-page blueprint for turning Alberta from a province into an independent country.

“We have everything. Alberta is an economic powerhouse. But we’re also on the ground with our face in our dirt and our arms tied behind our backs because of Ottawa,” he said, referring to a longstanding belief that the federal government continues to exert unfair influence over the oil-rich province. “That’s how many Albertans feel, and that’s why they want change.”

His blueprint, however, has drawn criticism for leaving major questions about the costs and practicalities of independence unresolved. The University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy recently estimated that the costs associated with separation could cost Alberta between C$50bn and C$170bn over its first five years and warned substantial annual deficits were possible.

Nor have the secessionists built the political machinery that could bring it about. The campaign has no official leader, nor an organised movement under the guise of a political party. No elected officials have campaigned for independence. Unlike Quebec, where independence parties have run explicitly on the idea and won, Alberta has only ever elected a separatist candidate once, and he lost his seat months later. In previous elections, separatist parties have won an average popular vote of 1%.

In the absence of coherent leadership, prominent figures have been thrust into the limelight, often with chaotic results. Jeff Rath, a bombastic lawyer linked to the Alberta Prosperity Project, is embroiled in legal battles over allegations that millions of dollars in disputed First Nations trust funds were mishandled. Mitch Sylvestre, head of the Alberta Prosperity Project and owner of a sporting goods store, told the Toronto Star he fears King Charles will have him assassinated. David Parker, a longtime rightwing political organizer, was at the centre of a voter-data scandal that exposed the personal information of nearly 3 million Albertans and remains under investigation.

But for Meikle and others, the movement is “grassroots” and would only be damaged by the presence of elected officials. “We just need our politicians to get out of the way and stop being so biased towards this movement,” he said. “They shouldn’t be using taxpayer money to campaign against us.”

For many here, the coronavirus pandemic remains an animating force. Some of the panellists and speakers were prominent lawyers who challenged and in some cases won cases against the government for overreach in shutdown laws.

It was the pandemic – and the political atmosphere that followed it – that got Betty Field, a retiree who worked in the oil sector, interested in the independence movement. Her husband, Gord Pick, chimed in that even supporters of federalism should vote against unity “to put a little fear of God into Ottawa”.

But the lack of a leader has led to divergence over messaging and strategy. In early October, the Globe and Mail reported on ties between the Alberta separatists movement and Republican operatives, and meetings between those unelected Albertans and White House staff. Among items allegedly discussed were oil revenues that could be directed to the US in exchange for assistance establishing a new country, as well as Alberta’s fresh water resources.
“We wouldn’t want to be part of the US,” said Pick. “Why trade one overlord in Ottawa for another in Washington?”

Outside, fresh off their weekly dinner of liver and onions – “just the best in Calgary, hands down!” – friends Vera Patten and Lisette Bourget stand in the waning sun, smoking a cigarette. When a conference attender offers to hold the door for them, Patten says politely: “Oh we’re not with you.”

“I hope they lose,” she adds after a small crowd, also out for a smoke, returns back inside. “It’s just disgusting. I can’t believe how they’re trying to break up this country.” A veteran of the oil industry, Patten has lived in Calgary for decades and says only damage can come from separation. “This needs to stop, and I’m hopeful that after the vote – that they lose.”
Wilson said the movement had other plans.

“The separatist movement in Alberta started before my parents were born – and they’re dead,” he said. “Because if you’re a separatist, you see a better opportunity for your friends, neighbours and your grandkids. And you never give up on that. Even if the vote goes poorly, it will not end. In the same way that winters won’t end and springs won’t end, this movement won’t end either. It’s here to stay.”

articles.title: ‘Clean air is not a favour’: Indonesia’s neighbours fed up with acrid haze as Singapore threatens to prosecute
articles.summary: Millions affected by smoke from wildfires as schools close, respiratory illnesses soar and diplomatic tensions rise
body: Singapore is threatening to prosecute companies responsible for some of the worst fires in years in neighbouring Indonesia, as the region grows increasingly frustrated with a persistent, acrid haze that could result in diplomatic relations fraying.

Lawrence Wong, the Singaporean prime minister, said his government was distributing masks to vulnerable citizens and working with countries in the region to deal with the smoke. “At the same time, we are looking into which companies may be responsible for the fires,” he said in a Facebook post on Thursday, adding that he was exploring the idea of “joint action with other countries”.
Related: ‘The physical toll is visceral’: How Indonesia’s fire haze affects millions - visual guide
Singapore has no plantations or forests of its own, but several companies with concessions in Indonesia are reportedly based in the city-state.

Haze is a persistent problem in Indonesia, but drier-than-usual conditions mean the thick smoke has been drifting into nearby Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei and Timor-Leste, and as far afield as the Philippines and Vietnam. Millions are affected, with school closures, respiratory illness spiking and air pollution indexes reaching unhealthy levels.
Malaysians and Singaporeans have been sharing images online of their cities, with skyscrapers disappearing into the smog, and frustration with the region’s most populous country is boiling over.

“Year after year, the haze comes back. It affects our health, closes schools, hurts businesses, and costs us billions,” a veteran Malaysian social activist and former politician wrote in a public letter this week. Lee Lam Thye said that real enforcement and “not just polite words” were needed. “Those responsible must be named, investigated, and punished. Clean air is not a favour. It is a basic right.”

While Indonesia regularly battles wildfires in the dry season, these blazes are the most intense in more than a decade and exacerbated by slash-and-burn practices to clear land for agriculture, including palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer.

Regional diplomats have offered to help Indonesia, but their offers have not always been immediately accepted. On Monday, an Indonesian official said the country was “still capable of handling it”. By the end of the week, Jakarta said it would accept assistance.

Such delicate diplomacy is routine among the region’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), which is built on ​quiet engagement and non-interference. A meeting of regional foreign ministers in the Philippines is due next month, but that might be too late.

Nerves are fraying. In remarks that went viral on social media, Syahganda Nainggolan, the head of Indonesia’s government communication agency, hit back at the criticism on Saturday. “We don’t only send haze,” he said, “the oxygen in Singapore and Malaysia comes from our forests.”

Rare strong words came earlier this month from Anwar Ibrahim, the Malaysian prime minister. He said he had been in contact with Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto, “who agreed to take the necessary steps, and this commitment must be followed by immediate and effective action from the Indonesian side to tackle the root causes of the haze”.
At the same time, pressure is growing on Jakarta to declare a national disaster, first from civil society groups but now also from Indonesian politicians and neighbours.

According to the Jakarta Post, Indonesian students have been holding protests across Kalimantan and Sumatra, demanding accountability and government action. In one video posted online, a child in a mask stands outside under a dark orange sky and calls on the local and national government to help. He holds a sign that says: “Save our little lungs”.
The country has dispatched firefighters and announced a crackdown on arsonists, but declaring a disaster would unlock funds and help thousands with medical expenses.
On Friday, the Indonesian forestry ministry said four firefighters were killed in a national park in Java.

Longtime onlookers say the issue is not just firefighting, but targeting the companies involved. In recent years, several attempts to take legal action against the companies exacerbating “transboundary haze” have failed, both locally and internationally, and posed a diplomatic minefield.

Haze is complex for Singapore and Malaysia, as they host companies working in Indonesia. A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia that it claimed were linked to burning land in Indonesia.

Ultimately, Indonesians bear the brunt of the blazes. The health ministry has reported nearly 280,000 people in the country with respiratory infections linked to the fires, with children under five accounting for more than 60,000.

Michelle Dyonisius, a campaigner at Amnesty International Indonesia, said rights groups and civil society organisations were ramping up pressure on the government to declare a national disaster emergency. “It has been going on for months, affecting millions and millions of people, including abroad,” she said.

“I think there is a refusal to acknowledge the gravity of the issue at hand and also the belief that it is under control. But considering the gravity of the issue and all of the people affected, it seems quite naive to remain in that position.”

articles.title: Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’
articles.summary: US president says Zelenskyy ‘more difficult ​to deal with ​than Putin’ after ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses
body: Donald Trump has called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy after an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.

Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries ⁠after Zelenskyy said Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire unilaterally declared by Trump on Sunday, having briefly halted its attacks to demonstrate its readiness for peace talks. Russia had continued its strikes on Ukrainian power plants.
Related: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses
In an interview with Newsmax aired on Thursday, the US president said: “All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace.

“There are a lot ‌of targets you can ‌hit, but when you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, ‌diesel oil, and we need that, and the world needs that, then he’s not doing a good service for the world.”
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since Trump announced an easing sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel on to global markets.

Zelenskyy criticised the agreement, which was widely interpreted as an attempt to curb high fuel prices before the US midterm elections, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than four and a half years ago. US efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.

Trump repeated to Newsmax his views of the two leaders involved in the conflict. “I’m not a big fan of Zelenskyy,” Trump said. “I think they actually both would like to see it ⁠end, but I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult ​to deal with ​than Putin.”

Arriving in Brussels to meet EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy did not comment on Trump’s latest remarks. He said he was “so thankful that we have such huge support from the EU” and its leaders, whom he described as “real leaders”.
He went on to say that Ukraine wanted to end the war as quickly as possible, but “we don’t see now signals from [the] Russian side that they are ready for this”.

Kyiv’s relationship with Washington was strained further this week when Ukraine said Starlink services had been restricted, in effect hobbling Ukrainian drone strike missions and crucial air defences with a flick of the switch.
During a visit to London this week, the Ukrainian president said the sudden restriction of Starlink had left him feeling personally betrayed by Trump and lamented losing a partner.
Related: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses

The British defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said on Thursday that his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, had assured him in a face-to-face meeting that the vital satellite communications system had been restored. In an interview with the BBC, he said it was unclear what had caused the disruption, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.”
Amid growing doubts about long-term US commitment to Ukraine, European leaders declared their support for Zelenskyy.

Standing alongside the Ukrainian leader in Brussels, the European Council president, António Costa, said Ukraine could “count on us not only to support you in war” but also in the path to negotiating EU membership.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU had supported Trump’s energy ceasefire, “but we have seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute” and instead had escalated its attacks. She said the EU intended to increase pressure on Russia, promising a 22nd round of sanctions, adding: “We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.”
The promise of further European sanctions against Russia comes weeks after the EU lifted sanctions against two prominent Russian oligarchs at the request of France and Luxembourg.
After meeting Zelenskyy, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said it was “crucial” that Ukraine received “all the means necessary to protect itself”.
The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, posted online: “I can reassure you, dear Ukrainian friends and President Zelenskyy: YOU ARE NOT ALONE.”
As Zelenskyy met Macron in Brussels, he said that the Kremlin had “launched yet another vile drone strike on Ukrainian energy infrastructure” in the city of Lutsk, which caused blackouts.
The Kremlin, meanwhile, accused Ukraine of derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes on refineries.

articles.title: Friday briefing: How Manchester City’s ​financial scandal could upend the whole football league
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: Manchester City’s disgrace reaches far beyond sport, exposing not just a crisis in football but also raising questions about foreign owned British institutions
body: Good morning. It’s a sporting scandal of colossal proportions, with the juiciest details still to come. Manchester City’s ascent from mediocre to majestic changed the landscape of British football. Now, that pace looks set to be matched by a sudden, plummeting fall.

The club has been found guilty of breaching football finance rules to the tune of hundreds of millions of pounds, with ramifications poised to spill far beyond Manchester (the club denies the allegations, and says it will appeal). Foreign state ownership makes this an international relations issue, not just a sporting one. The prime minister has been dragged into the sleaze-fest, and the stream of stories shows no sign of slowing. Meanwhile, the Mancunian club has the chutzpah to sit at the top of the Premier League, much to the repulsion of my Manchester United-supporting boyfriend.

With the help of Guardian football writer Jonathan Wilson, today’s First Edition delivers everything you need to know about the crisis engulfing the beautiful game, and believe me, this one’s not just for the footie fans. That’s after the headlines.

Ukraine | Wes Streeting urged the US to stand by Ukraine on his visit to the American capital and sought to cool tensions between the two countries in the wake of the Starlink row that is threatening to set back Kyiv’s war effort.

UK news | Jeffrey Donaldson has been sentenced to 15 years for sexual offences against two women who were children when he abused them, completing what was described as a “catastrophic descent into disgrace”.
Hacking | An Israeli advertising agency has been serving millions of online adverts that allow “zero-click” spyware to be used against targets, researchers at a Canadian university have said.
UK news | A woman has alleged Russell Brand told her “it’s just fun” as he raped her in a hotel room at the 1999 Labour party conference, a court has heard.
US news | Donald Trump has shelved a widely condemned plan to livestream the execution of a disabled man by firing squad.

To some (Manchester City fans, mostly), it was a sporting success story for the ages. After decades of underachievement, a middle-of-the-road club transformed into England’s best performing – and top title-winning – team. Others grumbled that City’s success was a sad indictment of the state of modern football. The club’s change in fortunes came shortly after they were bought by the Abu Dhabi United Group, a private equity group owned by the Gulf state’s vice president. Billionaires had already gutted the topflight of its heart, now governments with entire GDPs to burn had descended.

Except, of course, the cash injection at Manchester City breached strict Premier League limits. Financial fair play rules, introduced by the league in 2013, aimed to keep a lid on spending so that clubs – financed by, say, a fossil-fuel rich state – couldn’t simply spend billions for immediate dominance. Only, that’s precisely what Manchester City did. According to an independent panel, they secretly boosted their income by a staggering £900m between 2009 and 2018.

When he first flicked through the panel’s 40-page verdict summary, Wilson was surprised by the “incredibly strong language it used for a dry legal document”. The word “sham” is repeated eight times. “There was a clear sense that the panel felt systematically lied to by City,” says Wilson.
The real spice is likely to come in the yet-to-be-published appendices to the verdict, which will probably contain names, companies and detailed figures.

These recent revelations didn’t come out of nowhere. Back in November 2018, German newspaper Der Spiegel published a four-part series on Manchester City (“Bending the Rules to the Tune of Millions” was the first headline). The paper’s bombshell reporting was based on data released in The Football Leaks, a website containing millions of documents on allegedly murky financial transactions in the sport, made public by Portuguese whistleblower (and convicted hacker) Rui Pinto. UEFA conducted an investigation, and in 2020 found the club guilty, though the punishments (a two-year ban from European competitions and a €30m fine) were watered down on appeal. Meanwhile, Manchester City kept on winning.

“There was wide recognition that Manchester City had gotten away with it by dragging out the process,” Wilson tells me – the Court of Arbitration for Sport found the club showed a “blatant disregard” to Uefa’s investigation. “There was a sense then that football could not really handle situations like these,” Wilson says.Then, last month, the Premier League announcement came: Manchester City was guilty of 114 charges. It’s understood these offences correlate to information already in the public domain: that Manchester City inflated the value of sponsorship deals to channel extra cash into the club; that secret payments were made to senior club figures and player agents. These were a contravention of financial rules, and the club “made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate” Premier League investigations.
The club has maintained its innocence, and intends to appeal.

Even allowing time for Manchester City to appeal, a sanction decision is expected around Christmas. Fines, point-docking, transfer bans, suspension and expulsion are all being discussed, though Premier League rules dictate there’s no limit to the penalties that could be dished out. The sheer scale of the rule-breaking means there’s little precedent for comparison. Everton were docked six points for a £20 million rule breach. Apply the same metrics, and Manchester City would lose hundreds. Knocking that much off their tally in a single season is “functionally identical” to a much softer sentence, says Wilson. (Points reset every season, and last year, league-toppers Arsenal finished on just 85.)

“It leads to the conclusion that expulsion from the Premier League might be the only logical outcome,” says Wilson. He’d also like them stripped of their titles, and to see an investigation launched immediately into the club’s finances from 2018 until now.

Expulsion would be complicated. The complex structure of English football means if Manchester City did get booted out of the Premier League, there’s no guarantee the club would find a place in a lower league. And, even if it’s recommended by the panel, Premier League clubs would need to vote it through on a two-thirds majority. “That vote is unpredictable, as some club owners have business ties in Abu Dhabi or fear setting a precedent where clubs can vote out rivals,” says Wilson.
How worried should Man City be?

Off the pitch, there’s the prospect of civil litigation lingering too: Liverpool, Arsenal, Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur each submitted formal legal notices before a September 2024 deadline, which reserves them the right to claim compensation for losses caused by City’s rule breaches. When Everton breached financial rules in the 2021/22 season Burnley successfully claimed close to £40m from the Merseyside club. The sums at stake in this instance could be eye-watering. Plus there’s the prospect of possible criminal proceedings. Tom Forster KC, a financial crime barrister, suggested that Manchester City “has a great deal to be worried about on this front”.

Then there’s the political fallout, which is still taking shape. Andy Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester through this period, a time during which Abu Dhabi made serious investments in the city. “That can be viewed either as benevolent community building or as a calculated investment, expecting returns and local influence,” says Wilson. Either way, it’s not ideal for the new prime minister.

Plus, Burnham’s initial response to the judgment raised eyebrows, saying he’d be “really concerned” if the owners were forced to sell. “His skepticism of the charges sounded like comments from a fan on a message board rather than a measured politician,” says Wilson. Clarifications from Number 10 soon followed, and Burnham committed to publishing details of his dealings with Manchester City. Yesterday, he requested a “manual trawl” of records from his time as Greater Manchester Mayor, after two hospitality dinners with Manchester City’s chair were found to be absent from the combined authority’s digital register.
What does this mean for English football?

The ramifications for English football are clear. The Premier League faces a massive problem: the success of its top side is built on foul play. And not just between 2009 and 2018, Wilson reckons. “Even if we assume City complied cleanly after the leaks emerged, their success since remains predicated on that unfair advantage. That’s a lot of titles – and a lot of prize money – won under compromised conditions.

As it stands, this is “hugely damaging” to the Premier League’s reputation and fan trust, Wilson says. Football is the UK’s most popular sport, and is worth billions to the economy. If faith is lost in the sport, that’s a real problem. On the other hand, football is just a ballgame without the drama, spectacle and narrative – to which this debacle adds plenty. Especially, Wilson says, “if the outcome demonstrates that the Premier League is willing to enforce its regulations against even its most dominant team.”

But there’s a story much bigger than football here. Manchester City (and Saudi Arabia’s Newcastle United for that matter) aren’t the only British institutions quasi-owned by foreign governments. Qatar, Saudi and China own the bulk of Heathrow Airport; through state-owned EDF, France claims significant chunks of UK energy infrastructure. Royal Mail, meanwhile, is owned by a Czech billionaire; more than 70% of the English water industry is in foreign ownership.

“This case illustrates the extent of foreign state influence over major British institutions,” says Wilson, “tracing back to New Labour policies that encouraged foreign state investment without sufficient safeguards against geopolitical manipulation.” But, if the Premier League holds course, its response could be just as symbolic. “In a broader societal landscape where massive wealth often overrides accountability, this would represent a major British institution taking a stand to enforce rule of law and regulatory compliance.”

I don’t get a chance to dance these days. So I found Lyndsey Winship’s piece on which music is the best to get down to both absolutely fascinating and a potent reminder to get myself ‘out out’. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team

If you’ve used the term “greedflation” you’re borrowing a term from Isabella Weber, who is quickly becoming one of the most sought-after economists of her generation. Our own Michael Segalov interviewed her, and the piece out this morning provides a rare bit of hope. Poppy

The Guardian splashes on “Revealed: chancellor poised to raise taxes on banks in budget”. The Mail has “Dumb and dumber”, in reference to Labour’s education policy, and the Financial Times says “Merz stands by welfare reform overhaul as he vows to fight on”.

They say everyone’s got a book in them … but most of us have no idea how to even begin putting pen to paper. Helpfully, in this piece Madeleine Aggeler asks the experts on how to get started – and keep going.

From setting timelines to taking classes and writing even just a page at a time, it’s filled with great guidance, including this from novelist Christopher Moore on how to restart your abandoned opus: “Think about why it’s important to you to finish it.
